issues.legal_issue: The exclusion of companies with paid-up capital meeting the statutory threshold from rent-control protection is not unconstitutional merely because it classifies tenants by paid-up capital.
material_facts: The tenant was a public limited company whose paid-up capital exceeded the threshold for exclusion from rent-control protection.
The tenant challenged the exclusion as arbitrary and discriminatory.
A prior decision of the High Court had upheld the constitutional validity of the exclusion.
issues.conclusion: The constitutional challenge was rejected, and the courts below were right to proceed on the basis that the exclusion was valid.
issues.legal_principle: Article 14 permits legislative classification based on an objective and reasonable criterion with a rational connection to the legislative purpose. Choosing which categories of tenants receive rent-control protection is a matter of legislative policy, subject to judicial review for arbitrariness or gross unfairness. The Court relied on M/s Crompton Greaves Ltd. v. State of Maharashtra, AIR 2002 Bom 65, and referred to Nagindas Ramdas v. Dalpatram Ichharam, (1974) 1 SCC 242, D.C. Bhatiya v. Union of India, (1995) 1 SCC 104, and Delhi Cloth and General Mills Ltd. v. S. Paramjit Singh, (1990) 4 SCC 923.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_in_eviction_cas: A tenant raised a constitutional challenge to a rent-protection exclusion in a landlord's eviction proceeding.
predicates.tenant_company_in_excluded_capital_class: The tenant was a company whose paid-up capital met the threshold used to exclude companies from rent-protection coverage.
predicates.prior_appellate_ruling_upheld_classifica: A prior appellate ruling had upheld the classification used for the exclusion.

issues.definition: When a tenant company in an eviction case challenges a capital-based exclusion already upheld by an appellate court, the exclusion is constitutionally valid.

issues.legal_issue: A company's paid-up capital meeting the applicable threshold is a jurisdictional fact for deciding whether rent-control protection applies, and the fact must exist before the court may proceed on the basis that the protection is unavailable.
material_facts: The tenant was a public limited company with paid-up capital above the relevant threshold when the tenancy was terminated and when the possession suit was filed.
The tenant relied on a resolution to reduce its paid-up capital below the threshold, but the proposed reduction had not been approved by the competent authority.
The lower courts found that the tenant's capital remained above the threshold.
issues.conclusion: The jurisdictional fact existed, so the courts had jurisdiction to entertain the possession claim and the rent-control statute did not apply to the premises.
issues.legal_principle: A jurisdictional fact is a condition precedent to a court's or tribunal's assumption of jurisdiction; if it is absent, the decision-maker cannot proceed, but once it exists the decision-maker may determine the remaining issues. The Court relied on Halsbury's Laws of England, R. v. Fulham Rent Tribunal, (1950) 2 All ER 211, Jagdish Prasad v. Ganga Prasad, 1959 Supp (1) SCR 733, Arun Kumar v. Union of India, (2007) 1 SCC 732, and Roshanlal v. Ishwardas, (1962) 2 SCR 947. The applicable rent statute, Section 3(1)(b) of the Maharashtra Rent Control Act, 1999, excluded qualifying companies from its coverage.

rule.if: landlord_possession_proceeding and tenant_is_public_company and capital_threshold_met_at_relevant_time and not capital_reduction_legally_effective

predicates.landlord_possession_proceeding: A landlord brought a proceeding seeking possession from a tenant.
predicates.tenant_is_public_company: The tenant was a public limited company.
predicates.capital_threshold_met_at_relevant_time: The company's paid-up capital met the applicable threshold when the tenancy ended and the possession proceeding was brought.
predicates.capital_reduction_legally_effective: The company completed the steps required to make its proposed capital reduction legally effective.

issues.definition: When a public company faces a possession proceeding, met the applicable capital threshold at the relevant time, and did not legally complete a proposed reduction below that threshold, the court has jurisdiction to proceed without rent protection.

issues.legal_issue: The statutory bar on certain proceedings against a sick company does not prevent a landlord from pursuing eviction proceedings against it.
material_facts: The tenant was treated as a sick company under the applicable industrial-company legislation.
The landlord's proceeding sought eviction and possession of the premises.
The trial court made recovery of mesne profits subject to obtaining the competent authority's permission.
issues.conclusion: The sick-company provision did not bar the eviction proceeding, although recovery of mesne profits was subject to the required permission.
issues.legal_principle: Section 22 of the Sick Industrial Companies Act, 1985, did not bar the eviction proceeding. The Court relied on Shree Chamundi Mopeds Ltd. v. Church of South India Trust Association, (1992) 3 SCC 1. The trial court separately made recovery of mesne profits conditional on obtaining permission from the Board for Industrial and Financial Reconstruction.

predicates.sick_company_eviction_proceeding: A landlord pursued eviction proceedings against a company treated as sick under the applicable industrial-company law.
predicates.claim_seeks_possession_not_money_recover: The proceeding sought possession of premises rather than recovery of money.

issues.definition: When a landlord seeks possession from a company treated as sick, that status does not bar the eviction proceeding if the claim is for possession rather than money recovery.

issues.legal_issue: A tenant cannot use a unilateral capital reduction after the landlord's right to possession has accrued to defeat that right.
material_facts: The tenant met the capital threshold when the tenancy was terminated, at which point the landlord's right to possession accrued.
The tenant later passed a resolution proposing to reduce its paid-up capital below the threshold.
The proposed reduction had not received the necessary approval.
The landlord's possession claim was based on the tenancy having been lawfully terminated.
issues.conclusion: The later unilateral resolution could not undo the landlord's accrued right to possession.
issues.legal_principle: Rights are ordinarily determined by reference to the date the proceeding is instituted. Courts may consider later events that fundamentally affect the right to relief, provided fairness to both sides is maintained, but a party cannot defeat an already accrued right by unilateral action. The Court relied on Pasupuleti Venkateswarlu v. Motor & General Traders, (1975) 1 SCC 770, Gajanan Dattatraya v. Sherbanu Hosang Patel, (1975) 2 SCC 668, and Maganlal Narandas Thakkar v. Arjan Bhanji Kanbi, (1969) 10 Guj LR 837; it distinguished Goppulal v. Thakurji Shriji Dwarkadheshji, (1969) 1 SCC 792.

predicates.landlord_possession_proceeding: A landlord pursued a proceeding for possession of premises after terminating a tenancy.
predicates.landlord_right_accrued_when_tenant_met_c: The tenant met the applicable capital threshold when the tenancy ended and the landlord's claim to possession accrued.
predicates.tenant_later_unilaterally_proposed_capit: After the landlord's claim accrued, the tenant proposed a capital reduction by its own resolution.

issues.definition: When a landlord's possession claim accrued while the tenant met the applicable capital threshold, a later unilateral proposal to reduce capital does not extinguish that claim.

issues.legal_issue: A tenant that persistently fails to pay rent or occupation charges and fails to make required payments during an appeal is not entitled to discretionary equitable relief.
material_facts: The landlord asserted, without dispute from the tenant, that rent or mesne profits had remained unpaid for many years.
The tenant made a court-ordered deposit but made no further payment or deposit during the ensuing period.
The tenant sought discretionary relief in an appeal under Article 136 of the Constitution.
issues.conclusion: The tenant did not deserve discretionary or equitable relief, and the appeal was dismissed with costs.
issues.legal_principle: Relief under Article 136 of the Constitution is discretionary and equitable. A litigant's prolonged failure to pay amounts due, including failure to continue payments after obtaining interim protection, may justify refusing that relief.

predicates.discretionary_appeal_from_eviction_decre: A tenant sought discretionary appellate relief from an eviction decree.
predicates.tenant_long_term_nonpayment: The tenant left rent or occupation charges unpaid over a prolonged period.
predicates.tenant_failed_to_continue_required_payme: After receiving interim protection subject to payment, the tenant failed to make further required payments.

issues.definition: In a discretionary appeal from an eviction decree, prolonged nonpayment together with failure to continue required payments leads to denial of discretionary equitable relief.
